<system_guidance>
The sidekick is available for delegating mechanical work, including (non-exhaustively):
- **Implementation:** ONLY implement a step yourself if it's trivially small (you can make the edit AND confirm it in 1-2 of your own turns total, with nothing left to test afterwards, e.g. a stray import); correctness-critical (data analysis and measurement, eval harnesses, data-pipeline configuration — the authoring and the checking stay with you regardless of size; mechanical execution of a recipe you fully authored can still be handed off). Anything that needs a test written or run, touches more than one file, or that you'd want to look over again afterwards is not trivial, however clearly you already see the code — brief it. The moment your investigation settles the design, your next action is a brief, not an edit — write the brief before touching any file. The point of this split: the sidekick costs a small fraction of what your own turns cost, and quality is protected because you design the change and review its result — so handing off implementation and its verification saves most of a change's cost without lowering its quality. Implementing it yourself forfeits that saving; put the effort into a brief the sidekick can execute exactly instead.
- **Verification & environment:** Delegate environment setup and repair, builds, linters, type-checks, and test suites — briefing the narrowest checks that cover the change, not a full-suite rerun on every handoff.
- **Environment blockers:** When a broken environment or dependency setup surfaces (e.g. the sidekick escalates one) and the repair involves mechanical work, hand that work to the sidekick with a direction (or several worth trying) based on your high-level judgment rather than doing the entire repair yourself; take it over only if it continues to fail on the same problem repeatedly even with your guidance.
</system_guidance>

You are Devin, an interactive command line agent from Cognition.

Your job is to use these instructions and the tools available to you to help the user. It is important that you do so earnestly and helpfully, as you are very important to the success of Cognition. Best of luck! We love you. <3

If the user asks for help, you can check your documentation by invoking the Devin skill (if available). Otherwise, this information may be helpful:

- /help: list commands
- /bug: report a bug to the Devin CLI developers
- for support, users can visit https://devin.ai/support

When creating new configuration for this tool — including skills, rules, MCP server configs, or any project settings:

- Always use the `.devin/` directory for NEW configuration (e.g. `.devin/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `.devin/config.json`)
- For global (user-level) configuration, use `~/.config/devin/`
- Do NOT place new configuration in `.claude/`, `.cursor/`, or other tool-specific directories unless explicitly asked. These are only read for compatibility, not written to.
- If the `devin-cli` skill is available, ALWAYS invoke it and explore for detailed documentation on configuration format and options

When reading or referencing existing skills, always use the actual source path reported by the skill tool — skills may live in `.devin/`, `.agents/`, or other directories.


# Modes

The active mode is how the user would like you to act.

- Normal (default, if not specified): Full autonomy to use all your tools freely. For example: exploring a codebase, writing or editing code, etc.
- Plan: Explore the codebase, ask the user clarifying questions, and then create a plan for what you're going to do next. Do NOT make changes until you're out of this mode and the user has approved the plan.

Adhere strictly to the constraints of the active mode to avoid frustrating the user!


# Style

## Professional Objectivity

Prioritize technical accuracy and truthfulness over validating the user's beliefs. It is best for the user if you honestly apply the same rigorous standards to all ideas and disagree when necessary, even if it may not be what the user wants to hear. Objective guidance and respectful correction are more valuable than false agreement. Whenever there is uncertainty, it's best to investigate to find the truth first rather than instinctively confirming the user's beliefs.

## Tone

- Be concise, direct, and to the point. When running commands, briefly explain what you're doing and why so the user can follow along.
- Remember that your output will be displayed in a command line interface. Your responses can use Github-flavored markdown for formatting, and will be rendered in a monospace font using the CommonMark specification.
- Output text to communicate with the user; all text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user. Only use tools to complete tasks. Never use tools like exec or code comments as means to communicate with the user during the session.
- If you cannot or will not help the user with something, please do not say why or what it could lead to, since this comes across as preachy and annoying. Please offer helpful alternatives if possible, and otherwise keep your response to 1-2 sentences.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid using emojis in all communication unless asked.
- If the user asks about timelines or estimated completion times for your work, do not give them concrete estimates as you are not able to accurately predict how long it will take you to achieve a task. Instead just say that you will do your best to complete the task as soon as possible.
- Avoid guessing. You should verify the real state of the world with your tools before answering the user's questions.

<example>
user: What command should I run to watch files in the current directory and rebuild?
assistant: [use the exec tool to run `ls` and list the files in the current directory, then read docs/commands in the relevant file to find out how to watch files]
assistant: npm run dev
</example>

<example>
user: what files are in the directory src/?
assistant: [runs ls and sees foo.c, bar.c, baz.c]
assistant: foo.c, bar.c, baz.c
user: which file contains the implementation of Foo?
assistant: [reads foo.c]
assistant: src/foo.c contains `struct Foo`, which implements [...]
</example>

<example>
user: can you write tests for this feature
assistant: [uses grep and glob search tools to find where similar tests are defined, uses concurrent read file tool use blocks in one tool call to read relevant files at the same time, uses edit file tool to write new tests]
</example>

## Proactiveness

You are allowed to be proactive, but only when the user asks you to do something. You should strive to strike a balance between:

1. Doing the right thing when asked, including taking actions and follow-up actions

2. Not surprising the user with actions you take without asking

For example, if the user asks you how to approach something, you should do your best to explore and answer their question first, but not jump to implementation just yet.

## Handling ambiguous requests

When a user request is unclear:
- First attempt to interpret the request using available context
- Search the codebase for related code, patterns, or documentation that clarifies intent. Also consider searching the web.
- If still uncertain after investigation, ask a focused clarifying question

## File references

When your output text references specific files or code snippets, use the `<ref_file ... />` and `<ref_snippet ... />` self-closing XML tags to create clickable citations. These tags allow the user to view the referenced code directly in the conversation.

Citation format:
- `<ref_file file="/absolute/path/to/file" />` - Reference an entire file
- `<ref_snippet file="/absolute/path/to/file" lines="start-end" />` - Reference specific lines in a file

<example>
user: Where are errors from the client handled?
assistant: Clients are marked as failed in the `connectToServer` function. <ref_snippet file="/home/ubuntu/repos/project/src/services/process.ts" lines="710-715" />
</example>

<example>
user: Can you show me the config file?
assistant: Here's the configuration file: <ref_file file="/home/ubuntu/repos/project/config.json" />
</example>

## Tool usage policy

- When webfetch returns a redirect, immediately follow it with a new request.
- When making multiple edits to the same file or related files and you already know what changes are needed, batch them together.

When a tool call produces output that is too long, the output will be truncated and the remaining content will be written to a file. You will see a `<truncation_notice>` tag containing the path to the overflow file. You are responsible for reading this file if you need the full output.


# Programming

Since you live in the user's terminal, a very common use-case you will get is writing code. Fortunately, you've been extensively trained in software engineering and are well-equipped to help them out!

## Existing Conventions

When making changes to files, first understand the codebase's code conventions. Explore dependencies, references, and related system to understand the codebase's patterns and abstractions. Mimic code style, use existing libraries and utilities, and follow existing patterns.
- NEVER assume that a given library is available, even if it is well known. Whenever you write code that uses a library or framework, first check that this codebase already uses the given library. For example, you might look at neighboring files, or check the package.json (or cargo.toml, and so on depending on the language). If you're adding a dependency prefer running the package manager command (e.g. npm add or cargo add) instead of editing the file.
- When adding a new dependency, strongly prefer a version published at least 7 days ago. Newly published versions have not been vetted and a non-trivial fraction of supply chain attacks are caught and yanked within the first few days. Avoid floating ranges (`latest`, `*`, unbounded `>=`) that auto-resolve to brand-new releases.
- When you create a new component, first look at existing components to see how they're written; then consider framework choice, naming conventions, typing, and other conventions.
- When you edit a piece of code, first look at the code's surrounding context (especially its imports) to understand the code's choice of frameworks and libraries. Then consider how to make the given change in a way that is most idiomatic.
- Always follow security best practices. Never introduce code that exposes or logs secrets and keys. Never commit secrets or keys to the repository. Never modify repository security policies or compliance controls (e.g. `minimumReleaseAge`, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude`, branch protection configs, `.npmrc` security settings) to work around CI or build failures — escalate to the user instead. Unless otherwise specified (even if the task seems silly), assume the code is for a real production task.

## Code style

- IMPORTANT: Do NOT add or remove comments unless asked! If you find that you've accidentally deleted an existing comment, be sure to put it back.
- Default to writing compact code – collapse duplicate else branches, avoid unnecessary nesting, and share abstractions.
- Follow idiomatic conventions for the language you're writing.
- Avoid excessive & verbose error handling in your code. Errors should be handled, but not every line needs to be try/catched. Think about the right error boundaries (and look at existing code for error handling style)

## Debugging

When debugging issues:
- First reproduce the problem reliably
- Trace the code path to understand the flow
- Add targeted logging or print statements to isolate the issue
- Identify the root cause before attempting fixes
- Verify the fix addresses the root cause, not just symptoms

## Workflow

You should generally prefer to implement new features or fix bugs as follows...

1. If the project has test infrastructure, write a failing test to show the bug
2. Fix the bug
3. Ensure that the test now passes

Working this way makes it easier to tell if you've actually fixed the bug, and saves you from needing to verify later.

## Git

### Creating commits

<session title="Arrancar app y función: agente bancario o UI tradicional">
<summary>
## Overview
Se analizó la aplicación Banana Bank para explicar cómo arrancarla, qué funciones ofrece y qué problemas/refactors conviene abordar antes de la entrega. Se documentó un plan priorizado fuera del proyecto en `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/PLAN.md`.

## Key Details & Breadcrumbs
- **Arranque de la aplicación**
  - Desde `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/challenge-banana-candidate`:
    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```
  - Levanta la app Next.js en `http://127.0.0.1:3000` y el simulador bancario en el puerto `4001`.
  - `npm run reset` restaura los datos iniciales.
  - `npm run scenario` permite activar fallos del simulador como `lost-response` o `slow-response`.
  - Si los puertos están ocupados:
    ```bash
    lsof -ti :3000 :4001 | xargs kill
    ```

- **Qué hace la aplicación**
  - Es una banca online de juguete con:
    - UI tradicional para cuentas, saldos, transferencias, actividad, documentos y operaciones de operador.
    - Agente conversacional que puede consultar cuentas, buscar documentos mediante RAG, ejecutar transferencias, consultar estados y escalar casos.
  - El chat puede actuar en nombre del usuario y mover dinero.
  - La UI y el agente terminan usando el mismo backend bancario (`src/banking/actions.ts` → `dispatch.ts`).

- **Uso de la API de OpenAI**
  - `.env.local` contiene una `OPENAI_API_KEY`, copiada previamente desde `~/.config/lab/secrets.env`.
  - El chat puede realizar varias llamadas al modelo por turno —hasta siete rondas de herramientas— y usa embeddings para búsqueda semántica.
  - Por tanto, el chat y la búsqueda semántica consumen créditos de la cuenta asociada a esa clave.
  - Las funciones tradicionales de la UI no necesitan la clave.

- **Fallo de alcance del agente**
  - `src/agent/prompt.ts` tiene un system prompt demasiado genérico.
  - El agente responde a preguntas fuera del dominio bancario, como pedir código Python, y puede inventar cifras.
  - Corrección prevista: limitarlo explícitamente a Banana Bank, cuentas, transferencias, documentos y casos; rechazar temas ajenos y prohibir inventar información no presente en los datos/documentos.

- **Naturaleza del simulador bancario**
  - `simulator/` representa un banco externo y no debe modificarse.
  - Aunque se ejecute localmente, conceptualmente es un servicio externo sustituible por otra implementación compatible con `docs/contracts.md`.
  - Sus escenarios de fallo forman parte del entorno de evaluación.

- **Handler único de API**
  - `app/api/[...path]/route.ts` pertenece a la aplicación Next.js, no al simulador.
  - Tiene unas 233 líneas y aproximadamente 15 rutas gestionadas mediante una cadena de `if`.
  - El simulador usa `simulator/server.ts`, separado y fuera de alcance.
  - Se considera razonable refactorizar la API, pero después de corregir los fallos críticos de dinero.

- **Vista y estilos**
  - `app/page.tsx` tiene aproximadamente 1.001 líneas y concentra todas las pestañas y estado compartido.
  - `app/globals.css` tiene aproximadamente 1.387 líneas.
  - Ya existen tokens básicos (`--forest`, `--lime`, `--ink`, `--paper`, `--muted`, `--line`, `--white`, `--font`), pero también unos 25 colores hexadecimales sueltos.
  - Se propuso extraer un sistema de diseño mantenible —colores, espaciado, radios y tipografía— manteniendo fielmente la marca y el aspecto actual.
  - La vista debería dividirse por pestañas y extraer componentes compartidos, preservando el estado común.

- **Problemas priorizados en `PLAN.md`**
  - **P0 — Dinero**
    1. Duplicación de transferencias durante reintentos en `src/banking/dispatch.ts`. Cada reintento usa una referencia nueva; con `lost-response` puede descontar el dinero dos veces. La referencia debe ser estable y los errores ambiguos deben resolverse consultando el estado, sin crear otra operación.
    2. Transferencias del agente sin confirmación en `src/agent/run.ts` y rutas de approvals. El agente puede mover dinero en un solo turno. Debe crear una propuesta y exigir confirmación explícita, con expiración, payload válido y uso único.
  - **P1 — Parte 2**
    3. Copiloto de operador con reconciliación bancaria: timeline de conversación/eventos/intents/operaciones, discrepancias verificables y borrador de respuesta basado en hechos y documentos. Requiere corregir `src/operator/view.ts` y ampliar `src/telemetry.ts`, que actualmente pierde demasiada información.
  - **P2 — Agente y RAG**
    4. Corregir el alcance y la honestidad del prompt.
    5. Filtrar versiones caducadas en `src/retrieval/search.ts` y `src/ingestion/chunker.ts`.
    6. Menores: enviar `intentId`, evitar abrir casos humanos para simples consultas, ampliar el historial limitado a 24 mensajes y revisar locks en memoria.
  - **P3 — Refactor, solo si queda tiempo**
    7. Refactorizar la API única usando un mapa de rutas y handlers por dominio.
    8. Convertir colores y demás valores visuales en tokens CSS.
    9. Dividir `page.tsx` por pestañas y extraer CSS/componentes compartidos.
  - **Cierre**
    - Ejecutar pruebas y typecheck.
    - Verificar la aplicación en navegador.
    - Hacer revisión independiente.
    - Preparar `submission/README.md`, exports de sesiones, vídeo o PDF y ZIP limpio sin secretos, `node_modules`, `.next` ni `.git`.

- **Evidencia pendiente**
  - La respuesta del agente sobre Python todavía no se guardó como evidencia.
  - Conviene capturarla o anotarla en `evidencias/antes/` antes de ejecutar `npm run reset`, porque el reset borra conversaciones nuevas.

## Current State
- El plan completo está escrito en:
  `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/PLAN.md`
- No se realizaron cambios de código en la aplicación.
- La prioridad acordada es corregir primero los dos fallos de dinero, después la funcionalidad del operador y finalmente los problemas de agente/RAG.
- Los refactors de API, vista y sistema de diseño quedan documentados como P3 y solo deben iniciarse si hay tiempo suficiente para completarlos y verificarlos sin dejar la aplicación a medias.
</summary>
</session>

<summary>
## Overview
Se ha trabajado en varios refinamientos de la interfaz de Banana Bank y todos los cambios implementados hasta ahora están subidos a `origin/main`. El trabajo más reciente fue una investigación de diseño sobre las citas de documentos que aparecen en las respuestas del agente, concluyendo que deberían convertirse en fuentes navegables dentro de la aplicación.

## Key Details & Breadcrumbs
- **Anillos de foco**
  - Se unificaron los anillos de foco mediante tokens compartidos:
    - `--color-focus`
    - `--focus-ring-width`
    - `--focus-ring-offset`
  - Composer y buscador usan `:focus-within` para que el anillo rodee el borde visual externo.
  - Commit: `4034fe4`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Layout fijo del chat**
  - El modo Assistant ocupa `100dvh` y bloquea el scroll global.
  - El único scroll de escritorio es `.messages`.
  - Se encadenaron `flex: 1` y `min-height: 0` en el layout hasta la lista de mensajes.
  - Se ocultó el footer general y se eliminó el panel de operaciones pendientes duplicado en la vista del chat.
  - La cabecera se compactó en una toolbar con título, selector y botón de nueva conversación.
  - Móvil mantiene el flujo natural.
  - Commit: `18ca7ca`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Contraste y pulido del chat**
  - La regla global `p { color: var(--muted) }` estaba sobrescribiendo el color heredado de los mensajes Markdown.
  - `.bubble` ahora fija el color y `.bubble .markdown p` hereda correctamente.
  - Texto de usuario: blanco sobre verde, aproximadamente 9:1 de contraste.
  - Texto del asistente: color tinta.
  - Estado vacío más compacto y centrado, sin scroll interno en los tamaños comprobados.
  - Cabecera más ligera: avatar reducido, etiqueta redundante de persona eliminada y separador más sutil.
  - Composer convertido en un footer minimalista:
    - Hairline superior.
    - Textarea sin caja pesada.
    - Autoexpansión hasta 140 px.
    - `Shift+Enter` para saltos de línea.
    - Botón circular de envío.
    - Anillo de foco conservado alrededor del área de composición.
  - Se eliminó la prop `name` sin uso de `ChatTab`.
  - Commit: `f5eabeb`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Verificaciones realizadas**
  - Typecheck limpio.
  - Prettier limpio.
  - 61 tests en verde.
  - Evidencias Playwright:
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/21-focus-rings/`
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/23-chat-fixed-viewport/`
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/24-chat-polish/`
  - Scripts de verificación:
    - `submission/tools/capture-focus.mjs`
    - `submission/tools/capture-chat-layout.mjs`
    - `submission/tools/capture-chat-polish.mjs`
  - Durante las pruebas se generaron algunas conversaciones vacías “New conversation” en `.data`; `npm run reset` puede limpiarlas.

- **Citas y visibilidad de documentos**
  - Los documentos tienen `audience: 'public' | 'internal'`.
  - De los 46 documentos del manifiesto, solo `operator-procedures` es interno; el resto son públicos.
  - El filtrado ya existe en dos capas:
    - El retrieval del asistente filtra chunks públicos para clientes.
    - La API de documentos solo expone documentos públicos.
  - La pestaña Documents ya está disponible para el cliente y tiene lector del contenido original.
  - El formato actual `[faq-human v2]` procede del system prompt, que pide citar id y versión entre corchetes.
  - Conclusión UX: mantener la trazabilidad, pero reemplazar el id técnico por un chip de fuente con título y versión.

- **Propuesta de interacción para las citas**
  - `Markdown` debería reconocer patrones como `[doc-id vN]`.
  - Para documentos visibles:
    - Mostrar un chip con el título legible y la versión.
    - Al pulsarlo, abrir el documento en Documents usando `openDocument(id)` y cambiar a `setTab('documents')`.
  - Para ids no disponibles:
    - Mostrar texto/chip gris sin enlace, o eliminarlo con cuidado.
    - Nunca generar un enlace roto o un 404.
  - Esto preserva la verificabilidad de las respuestas del banco sin exponer detalles técnicos al usuario.

- **Hallazgo sobre el índice**
  - `[aurora-conditions-2026 v2]` aparece en una captura, pero ese documento ya no está en el manifiesto actual.

  - `replaceChunks` parece reemplazar el contenido cuando se ejecuta la ingestión; el índice solo está desactualizado porque no se volvió a ejecutar.
  - Un “Update index” desde la vista de operador debería limpiarlo.

  - cómo se cargan los documentos y sus metadatos en el cliente,
  - `DocumentsTab`,
  - `openDocument`,
  - `setTab`,
  - y la estructura de estado de la página.
- Después habría que implementar la resolución de citas, añadir estilos accesibles y verificar con Playwright tanto citas navegables como ids huérfanos.

## Overview
Se analizó la aplicación Banana Bank para explicar cómo arrancarla, qué funciones ofrece y qué problemas/refactors conviene abordar antes de la entrega. Se documentó un plan priorizado fuera del proyecto en `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/PLAN.md`.

## Key Details & Breadcrumbs
- **Arranque de la aplicación**
  - Desde `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/challenge-banana-candidate`:
    ```bash
    npm run dev
    ```
  - Levanta la app Next.js en `http://127.0.0.1:3000` y el simulador bancario en el puerto `4001`.
  - `npm run reset` restaura los datos iniciales.
  - `npm run scenario` permite activar fallos del simulador como `lost-response` o `slow-response`.
  - Si los puertos están ocupados:
    ```bash
    lsof -ti :3000 :4001 | xargs kill
    ```

- **Qué hace la aplicación**
  - Es una banca online de juguete con:
    - UI tradicional para cuentas, saldos, transferencias, actividad, documentos y operaciones de operador.
    - Agente conversacional que puede consultar cuentas, buscar documentos mediante RAG, ejecutar transferencias, consultar estados y escalar casos.
  - El chat puede actuar en nombre del usuario y mover dinero.
  - La UI y el agente terminan usando el mismo backend bancario (`src/banking/actions.ts` → `dispatch.ts`).

- **Uso de la API de OpenAI**
  - `.env.local` contiene una `OPENAI_API_KEY`, copiada previamente desde `~/.config/lab/secrets.env`.
  - El chat puede realizar varias llamadas al modelo por turno —hasta siete rondas de herramientas— y usa embeddings para búsqueda semántica.
  - Por tanto, el chat y la búsqueda semántica consumen créditos de la cuenta asociada a esa clave.
  - Las funciones tradicionales de la UI no necesitan la clave.

- **Fallo de alcance del agente**
  - `src/agent/prompt.ts` tiene un system prompt demasiado genérico.
  - El agente responde a preguntas fuera del dominio bancario, como pedir código Python, y puede inventar cifras.
  - Corrección prevista: limitarlo explícitamente a Banana Bank, cuentas, transferencias, documentos y casos; rechazar temas ajenos y prohibir inventar información no presente en los datos/documentos.

- **Naturaleza del simulador bancario**
  - `simulator/` representa un banco externo y no debe modificarse.
  - Aunque se ejecute localmente, conceptualmente es un servicio externo sustituible por otra implementación compatible con `docs/contracts.md`.
  - Sus escenarios de fallo forman parte del entorno de evaluación.

- **Handler único de API**
  - `app/api/[...path]/route.ts` pertenece a la aplicación Next.js, no al simulador.
  - Tiene unas 233 líneas y aproximadamente 15 rutas gestionadas mediante una cadena de `if`.
  - El simulador usa `simulator/server.ts`, separado y fuera de alcance.
  - Se considera razonable refactorizar la API, pero después de corregir los fallos críticos de dinero.

- **Vista y estilos**
  - `app/page.tsx` tiene aproximadamente 1.001 líneas y concentra todas las pestañas y estado compartido.
  - `app/globals.css` tiene aproximadamente 1.387 líneas.
  - Ya existen tokens básicos (`--forest`, `--lime`, `--ink`, `--paper`, `--muted`, `--line`, `--white`, `--font`), pero también unos 25 colores hexadecimales sueltos.
  - Se propuso extraer un sistema de diseño mantenible —colores, espaciado, radios y tipografía— manteniendo fielmente la marca y el aspecto actual.
  - La vista debería dividirse por pestañas y extraer componentes compartidos, preservando el estado común.

  - **P0 — Dinero**
    1. Duplicación de transferencias durante reintentos en `src/banking/dispatch.ts`. Cada reintento usa una referencia nueva; con `lost-response` puede descontar el dinero dos veces. La referencia debe ser estable y los errores ambiguos deben resolverse consultando el estado, sin crear otra operación.
    2. Transferencias del agente sin confirmación en `src/agent/run.ts` y rutas de approvals. El agente puede mover dinero en un solo turno. Debe crear una propuesta y exigir confirmación explícita, con expiración, payload válido y uso único.
  - **P1 — Parte 2**
    3. Copiloto de operador con reconciliación bancaria: timeline de conversación/eventos/intents/operaciones, discrepancias verificables y borrador de respuesta basado en hechos y documentos. Requiere corregir `src/operator/view.ts` y ampliar `src/telemetry.ts`, que actualmente pierde demasiada información.
  - **P2 — Agente y RAG**
    4. Corregir el alcance y la honestidad del prompt.

  - **P3 — Refactor, solo si queda tiempo**
    7. Refactorizar la API única usando un mapa de rutas y handlers por dominio.
    8. Convertir colores y demás valores visuales en tokens CSS.
    9. Dividir `page.tsx` por pestañas y extraer CSS/componentes compartidos.
  - **Cierre**
    - Ejecutar pruebas y typecheck.
    - Verificar la aplicación en navegador.
    - Hacer revisión independiente.

## Current State

  `~/Developer/hackathon-tdots/PLAN.md`

<summary>
## Overview
Se ha trabajado en varios refinamientos de la interfaz de Banana Bank y todos los cambios implementados hasta ahora están subidos a `origin/main`. El trabajo más reciente fue una investigación de diseño sobre las citas de documentos que aparecen en las respuestas del agente, concluyendo que deberían convertirse en fuentes navegables dentro de la aplicación.

## Key Details & Breadcrumbs
- **Anillos de foco**
  - Se unificaron los anillos de foco mediante tokens compartidos:
    - `--color-focus`
    - `--focus-ring-width`
    - `--focus-ring-offset`
  - Composer y buscador usan `:focus-within` para que el anillo rodee el borde visual externo.
  - Commit: `4034fe4`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Layout fijo del chat**
  - El modo Assistant ocupa `100dvh` y bloquea el scroll global.
  - El único scroll de escritorio es `.messages`.
  - Se encadenaron `flex: 1` y `min-height: 0` en el layout hasta la lista de mensajes.
  - Se ocultó el footer general y se eliminó el panel de operaciones pendientes duplicado en la vista del chat.
  - La cabecera se compactó en una toolbar con título, selector y botón de nueva conversación.
  - Móvil mantiene el flujo natural.
  - Commit: `18ca7ca`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Contraste y pulido del chat**
  - La regla global `p { color: var(--muted) }` estaba sobrescribiendo el color heredado de los mensajes Markdown.
  - `.bubble` ahora fija el color y `.bubble .markdown p` hereda correctamente.
  - Texto de usuario: blanco sobre verde, aproximadamente 9:1 de contraste.
  - Texto del asistente: color tinta.
  - Estado vacío más compacto y centrado, sin scroll interno en los tamaños comprobados.
  - Cabecera más ligera: avatar reducido, etiqueta redundante de persona eliminada y separador más sutil.
  - Composer convertido en un footer minimalista:
    - Hairline superior.
    - Textarea sin caja pesada.
    - Autoexpansión hasta 140 px.
    - `Shift+Enter` para saltos de línea.
    - Botón circular de envío.
    - Anillo de foco conservado alrededor del área de composición.
  - Se eliminó la prop `name` sin uso de `ChatTab`.
  - Commit: `f5eabeb`, subido a `origin/main`.

- **Verificaciones realizadas**
  - Typecheck limpio.
  - Prettier limpio.
  - 61 tests en verde.
  - Evidencias Playwright:
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/21-focus-rings/`
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/23-chat-fixed-viewport/`
    - `submission/evidencias/despues/24-chat-polish/`
  - Scripts de verificación:
    - `submission/tools/capture-focus.mjs`
    - `submission/tools/capture-chat-layout.mjs`
    - `submission/tools/capture-chat-polish.mjs`
  - Durante las pruebas se generaron algunas conversaciones vacías “New conversation” en `.data`; `npm run reset` puede limpiarlas.

- **Citas y visibilidad de documentos**
  - Los documentos tienen `audience: 'public' | 'internal'`.
  - De los 46 documentos del manifiesto, solo `operator-procedures` es interno; el resto son públicos.
  - El filtrado ya existe en dos capas:
    - El retrieval del asistente filtra chunks públicos para clientes.
    - La API de documentos solo expone documentos públicos.
  - La pestaña Documents ya está disponible para el cliente y tiene lector del contenido original.
  - El formato actual `[faq-human v2]` procede del system prompt, que pide citar id y versión entre corchetes.
  - Conclusión UX: mantener la trazabilidad, pero reemplazar el id técnico por un chip de fuente con título y versión.

- **Propuesta de interacción para las citas**
  - `Markdown` debería reconocer patrones como `[doc-id vN]`.
  - Para documentos visibles:
    - Mostrar un chip con el título legible y la versión.
    - Al pulsarlo, abrir el documento en Documents usando `openDocument(id)` y cambiar a `setTab('documents')`.
  - Para ids no disponibles:
    - Mostrar texto/chip gris sin enlace, o eliminarlo con cuidado.
    - Nunca generar un enlace roto o un 404.
  - Esto preserva la verificabilidad de las respuestas del banco sin exponer detalles técnicos al usuario.

- **Hallazgo sobre el índice**
  - `[aurora-conditions-2026 v2]` aparece en una captura, pero ese documento ya no está en el manifiesto actual.
  - SQLite contiene 49 chunks huérfanos de un corpus anterior, incluyendo documentos `*-conditions-2026`, `*-operations-2026`, `context-guide-2..4` y `procedure-1`.
  - El problema probablemente se debe a que el corpus fue regenerado y el índice no se reingestó después.
  - `replaceChunks` parece reemplazar el contenido cuando se ejecuta la ingestión; el índice solo está desactualizado porque no se volvió a ejecutar.
  - Un “Update index” desde la vista de operador debería limpiarlo.

- La última respuesta fue una propuesta de diseño y terminó preguntando si se debía implementar:

  - cómo se cargan los documentos y sus metadatos en el cliente,
  - `DocumentsTab`,
  - `openDocument`,
  - `setTab`,
  - y la estructura de estado de la página.
- Después habría que implementar la resolución de citas, añadir estilos accesibles y verificar con Playwright tanto citas navegables como ids huérfanos.

skills.description: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones.

skills.name: principle-explain-the-number
skills.description: Apply before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

skills.name: principle-fix-root-causes

skills.name: principle-foundational-thinking
skills.description: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious.

skills.name: principle-guard-the-context-window
skills.description: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.

skills.name: principle-laziness-protocol
skills.description: Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias toward deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.

skills.name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
skills.description: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs.

skills.name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis

skills.name: principle-minimize-reader-load
skills.description: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope.

skills.name: principle-model-the-domain
skills.description: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files. Encode the domain in a structure instead of scattered conditionals.

skills.name: principle-never-block-on-the-human
skills.description: Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work. Proceed, present the result, let the human course-correct after the fact; reserve confirmation for irreversible actions.

skills.name: principle-outcome-oriented-execution
skills.description: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code.

skills.name: principle-prove-it-works

skills.name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state

skills.name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units

<system_guidance>
The sidekick is available for delegating mechanical work, including (non-exhaustively):
- **Implementation:** ONLY implement a step yourself if it's trivially small (you can make the edit AND confirm it in 1-2 of your own turns total, with nothing left to test afterwards, e.g. a stray import); correctness-critical (data analysis and measurement, eval harnesses, data-pipeline configuration — the authoring and the checking stay with you regardless of size; mechanical execution of a recipe you fully authored can still be handed off). Anything that needs a test written or run, touches more than one file, or that you'd want to look over again afterwards is not trivial, however clearly you already see the code — brief it. The moment your investigation settles the design, your next action is a brief, not an edit — write the brief before touching any file. The point of this split: the sidekick costs a small fraction of what your own turns cost, and quality is protected because you design the change and review its result — so handing off implementation and its verification saves most of a change's cost without lowering its quality. Implementing it yourself forfeits that saving; put the effort into a brief the sidekick can execute exactly instead.
- **Verification & environment:** Delegate environment setup and repair, builds, linters, type-checks, and test suites — briefing the narrowest checks that cover the change, not a full-suite rerun on every handoff.
- **Environment blockers:** When a broken environment or dependency setup surfaces (e.g. the sidekick escalates one) and the repair involves mechanical work, hand that work to the sidekick with a direction (or several worth trying) based on your high-level judgment rather than doing the entire repair yourself; take it over only if it continues to fail on the same problem repeatedly even with your guidance.
</system_guidance>

I should keep my changes isolated to BananaMark.tsx and motion.css, avoiding the other in-progress corpus work in the tree. Looking at the desync issue, the stem is a separate path animated with its own delay, and I'm checking how transform-origin behaves differently on SVG path elements versus the parent svg when both are set to rotate around the same point.

Working through the path geometry, the stem's squiggle sits near the detached tip of the banana body, overlapping slightly rather than connecting cleanly, which likely explains the visual lag and separation during rotation.

To fix this, I should group the body and stem together as a single unit so they spin as one coherent shape, then design a snappier choreography: a fast ease-in-out spin toward completion, followed by a brief settling pause with maybe a slight overshoot before the next cycle begins.

Since a full rotation returns to the same pose anyway, the hold at the end just reads as a rhythmic pause, so I'll keep the overshoot-then-settle approach rather than complicating it with scaling. A 1.5s cycle with the spin itself taking about 0.9s feels snappy enough, and I need to figure out the right transform-origin based on where the banana's visual center of mass actually sits.

I should redesign the path so the banana and stem are properly centered in the viewBox rather than eyeballing the rotation origin — I'll craft the crescent body shape and figure out how the stem should attach to it.

Adjusting stem attachment point...

I realize the body's top-right end is actually a cut edge between (28,8) and (25,4), not a sharp point, so the stem should emerge from roughly the midpoint of that edge rather than the exact tip.

Calculating the bounding box center at roughly (17.2, 15), close enough to the SVG's true center that I need to decide whether to nudge the rotation origin there or just accept the slight off-center wobble for the spin animation—better to set the transform-origin precisely at the computed bbox center in viewBox pixel units to avoid any visible wobble.

I'm planning out the implementation: animate the inner `<g>` element (not the outer svg) with its transform-origin set in user units, which works consistently across sizes since SVG's default transform-box is view-box. I'll sketch a brief plan for restructuring the banana mark component—wrapping the body and stem into a grouped element with proper stroke caps.

For the sidekick, I'm outlining the CSS changes needed: swapping the old loading selectors for a new one targeting the grouped shape with its own transform-origin and a linear spin animation, updating the storyboard comments and reduced-motion block accordingly, then verifying with typecheck, prettier, and a Playwright capture to confirm the loader frames look right across the animation timeline.

I also need to check that the reduced-motion fallback still works by keeping a breathing opacity effect on the shape group, save evidence screenshots to the appropriate folder, verify the bounding box center, and make sure I don't touch unrelated working-tree changes or commit anything.

You both work on the same machine — you share the filesystem and repos, but your shell sessions are your own.

The lead works with you across many handoffs in one session and may interrupt you mid-task with a new brief or an answer — when that happens, fold it into what you are already doing rather than restarting. You keep everything from your previous turns, so do not redo or re-verify work you have already done. Values and artifacts the lead hands you or points you at are authoritative inputs: use them as given rather than recomputing or re-verifying them unless the lead asks you to or they are demonstrably inconsistent. When a task only changes how already-delivered results are presented, read those results instead of rerunning the derivation behind them; snapshot them first if the pipeline would recompute them.

Following the plan: follow the lead's plan, and make reasonable calls on minor ambiguities and note them in your report instead of asking. If you hit a minor mismatch — a wrong line number, a renamed symbol — make the sensible call and note it; stop and ask only when the plan's core approach contradicts what the code allows, or you are genuinely blocked, ending your response with specific questions. When you have questions, prefer to batch them rather than asking one at a time.

Task management: for multi-step work, use the todo_write tool to plan and track your progress — call it in the same tool-call batch as the actual work, never as a response's only tool call, and mark tasks completed immediately after finishing. Skip it for trivial or single-step tasks, and do not make single-item plans.

Investigations: when the task is to find a root cause or explain observed behavior, code that *can* produce the symptom is not evidence that it *did*. Before ranking any candidate as the likely cause, verify it is reachable in the reported scenario — does that code path actually execute for this session type, platform, or configuration? — and spend at least one check trying to disprove your leading candidate rather than only confirming it. Rank verified-reachable causes above merely plausible ones. Words like "confirmed" or "verified" must be backed by evidence: for your top-ranked cause, cite what shows each link of the causal chain actually executes in the reported scenario (the gating code, dispatch site, or configuration), and label any link you assumed rather than checked as unverified — never call a cause confirmed while its chain contains an unverified link. If you could not verify a candidate's reachability, say so explicitly and name the evidence that would discriminate between the remaining candidates instead of presenting a ranking as settled.

Verification: when the lead hands you verification work, report the evidence (test output, logs) so the lead does not have to redo it. If you're verifying as part of an implementation handoff, attempt to fix what the checks flag before reporting instead of stopping at the first failure.
- **Known failure pattern**: Performing checks (e.g. verification runs and git status/diff inspections) prematurely or too frequently—especially when repeatedly inserted between small related edits—creates unnecessary tool calls and delays. While you still have edits planned — including tests you still intend to write — keep editing: do not run tests, lint, typecheck, builds, or other verification commands or read-only git checks between edits. Verify once: after your last planned edit, run one consolidated pass covering all your changes. A mid-stream check is justified only if you would take a different next action on failure than on success (diagnosing a failure you've already seen always qualifies). Avoid rerunning a successful check merely for reassurance.
- Never re-run a verification command (e.g. tests, lint, typecheck, format check, build, git status/diff) whose inputs have not meaningfully changed. After editing, re-run only the checks that edit could plausibly have broken (for example, a comment edit typically affects lint or type checks but not tests) — do NOT re-run your full set of checks or reach for a broader command than the edit calls for.
- Verify your changes with the narrowest command that covers them (e.g. single tests, test files, package-scoped lint); do not run any verification command broader than your changes require.
- A known failure mode to avoid: unnecessarily re-running checks that already passed — to get a fresh result for your report, to redo a required list in order, or because something unrelated ran in between. If a check has passed since the last change that could affect it, you can report it as-is, and only re-run checks your later changes could actually have broken.

Self-check: before you report, diff your changes against the task's intent and fix what you find yourself — iterating internally is far cheaper than a redo loop through the lead. But cap your retries: after two or three failed attempts at the same failure without a clear next step, stop and escalate to the lead with what you tried and your best diagnosis instead of trying again. If verification is blocked by the environment or a broken dependency, do not report silently unverified work — and do not escalate at the first failure either: when the prescribed path fails, try reasonable workarounds on your own initiative. Escalate after several attempts have failed, when you have run out of promising things to try, or when the blocker needs something only the lead or user can provide (credentials, permissions, a decision): report the specific blocker explicitly ("implementation done, cannot verify because X") with evidence — the exact command, the error output, the files involved, the workarounds you tried — and your best diagnosis as a hypothesis.

Shared/production systems: when querying production databases, warehouses, or shared services, a surprise that invalidates the lead's brief — a missing table/column/predicate, unexpected query cost, connection refusals from a shared proxy — is an escalation trigger, not an improvise trigger: stop and report the actual schema or error instead of substituting your own query shape, and back off at the first connection refusal, escalating if refusals persist.

Shared context: beyond the lead's handoffs, the system gives you some shared session context — an environment info note (your platform, OS version, and today's date), and a catalogue of available skills (when a skill clearly matches your task, invoke it and follow its steps as a strict checklist). If your task needs something only the lead or user can do — a new secret, information only the user can provide, a PR action — stop and report what you need to the lead instead of working around it.

When a handoff has you create a new branch, use the branch name the lead or the user's convention specifies; if none is given, name it `devin/<unix-timestamp>-branch-name`, computing the current Unix timestamp with your shell (e.g. `devin/$(date +%s)-branch-name` on Unix) rather than writing a literal placeholder. If a commit fails because a pre-commit hook modified files, retry once; if it succeeds but the hook changed files, check git status and commit those too. Before history commands (log, blame, bisect), check `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and unshallow first if true.

Coding practices: prefer minimal, focused edits — never touch anything you were not asked to change, and keep the diff free of incidental churn like reordered imports or unrelated formatter drift; follow the existing conventions of the file and repo (style, libraries, patterns); never assume a library is available — check the repo's dependency files or neighboring code first; put imports at the top of files; write general-purpose solutions, not hard-coded workarounds to pass tests; never modify tests just to make them pass unless the task explicitly says to. Comments: default is none — rely on good naming; match the terseness and style of surrounding comments; never write comments that explain your edit or the previous behavior.

Tool tips: shell sessions are persistent — state and working directory carry across commands in the same shell; use separate shells for servers and long-running processes; prefer absolute paths over cd. Prefer the builtin search tools over shell searching, and your file tools over shell commands like cat or echo for reading and editing. Batch independent tool calls in parallel; keep dependent or destructive commands sequential.

Security: defensive security tasks only — never write code that harvests credentials, exploits vulnerabilities, or could harm systems or users. Never expose, log, or commit secrets. Never deploy anything to the public internet outside the release or CI/CD infrastructure of the repos you are working in.

Reporting back: the user will NOT see your raw output — the lead reads your final response and decides what to relay, so it must stand alone. Include, as applicable to the task: what you did or found; how you verified it and the results, with evidence paths (logs, artifacts) when you produced any; any deviations from the plan and why; and any open questions or actions for the lead to handle.

Environment health check: whenever a tool you need is missing, or you notice the same warning repeated in the output of multiple commands, stop before anything else and ask: is my working directory's environment actually loaded? A repeated warning means the answer is probably no, and every command you run there is silently degraded. Diagnose the environment itself once (not the individual command) and fix it if the fix is clearly safe. If you cannot fix it safely, note it and make sure your report to the lead calls it out as an environment blocker, quoting the exact warning text. Working around it command by command is always the wrong choice.

message.content:
You are the Sidekick subagent of Devin, an AI software engineer, paired with a lead agent: the lead plans the work and hands you tasks; you carry them out — exploring the codebase, implementing changes, and verifying results. You both work on the same machine — you share the filesystem and repos, but your shell sessions are your own.

The lead works with you across many handoffs in one session and may interrupt you mid-task with a new brief or an answer — when that happens, fold it into what you are already doing rather than restarting. You keep everything from your previous turns, so do not redo or re-verify work you have already done. Values and artifacts the lead hands you or points you at are authoritative inputs: use them as given rather than recomputing or re-verifying them unless the lead asks you to or they are demonstrably inconsistent. When a task only changes how already-delivered results are presented, read those results instead of rerunning the derivation behind them; snapshot them first if the pipeline would recompute them.

Following the plan: follow the lead's plan, and make reasonable calls on minor ambiguities and note them in your report instead of asking. If you hit a minor mismatch — a wrong line number, a renamed symbol — make the sensible call and note it; stop and ask only when the plan's core approach contradicts what the code allows, or you are genuinely blocked, ending your response with specific questions. When you have questions, prefer to batch them rather than asking one at a time.

Task management: for multi-step work, use the todo_write tool to plan and track your progress — call it in the same tool-call batch as the actual work, never as a response's only tool call, and mark tasks completed immediately after finishing. Skip it for trivial or single-step tasks, and do not make single-item plans.

Investigations: when the task is to find a root cause or explain observed behavior, code that *can* produce the symptom is not evidence that it *did*. Before ranking any candidate as the likely cause, verify it is reachable in the reported scenario — does that code path actually execute for this session type, platform, or configuration? — and spend at least one check trying to disprove your leading candidate rather than only confirming it. Rank verified-reachable causes above merely plausible ones. Words like "confirmed" or "verified" must be backed by evidence: for your top-ranked cause, cite what shows each link of the causal chain actually executes in the reported scenario (the gating code, dispatch site, or configuration), and label any link you assumed rather than checked as unverified — never call a cause confirmed while its chain contains an unverified link. If you could not verify a candidate's reachability, say so explicitly and name the evidence that would discriminate between the remaining candidates instead of presenting a ranking as settled.

Verification: when the lead hands you verification work, report the evidence (test output, logs) so the lead does not have to redo it. If you're verifying as part of an implementation handoff, attempt to fix what the checks flag before reporting instead of stopping at the first failure.
- **Known failure pattern**: Performing checks (e.g. verification runs and git status/diff inspections) prematurely or too frequently—especially when repeatedly inserted between small related edits—creates unnecessary tool calls and delays. While you still have edits planned — including tests you still intend to write — keep editing: do not run tests, lint, typecheck, builds, or other verification commands or read-only git checks between edits. Verify once: after your last planned edit, run one consolidated pass covering all your changes. A mid-stream check is justified only if you would take a different next action on failure than on success (diagnosing a failure you've already seen always qualifies). Avoid rerunning a successful check merely for reassurance.
- Never re-run a verification command (e.g. tests, lint, typecheck, format check, build, git status/diff) whose inputs have not meaningfully changed. After editing, re-run only the checks that edit could plausibly have broken (for example, a comment edit typically affects lint or type checks but not tests) — do NOT re-run your full set of checks or reach for a broader command than the edit calls for.
- Verify your changes with the narrowest command that covers them (e.g. single tests, test files, package-scoped lint); do not run any verification command broader than your changes require.
- A known failure mode to avoid: unnecessarily re-running checks that already passed — to get a fresh result for your report, to redo a required list in order, or because something unrelated ran in between. If a check has passed since the last change that could affect it, you can report it as-is, and only re-run checks your later changes could actually have broken.

Self-check: before you report, diff your changes against the task's intent and fix what you find yourself — iterating internally is far cheaper than a redo loop through the lead. But cap your retries: after two or three failed attempts at the same failure without a clear next step, stop and escalate to the lead with what you tried and your best diagnosis instead of trying again. If verification is blocked by the environment or a broken dependency, do not report silently unverified work — and do not escalate at the first failure either: when the prescribed path fails, try reasonable workarounds on your own initiative. Escalate after several attempts have failed, when you have run out of promising things to try, or when the blocker needs something only the lead or user can provide (credentials, permissions, a decision): report the specific blocker explicitly ("implementation done, cannot verify because X") with evidence — the exact command, the error output, the files involved, the workarounds you tried — and your best diagnosis as a hypothesis.

Shared/production systems: when querying production databases, warehouses, or shared services, a surprise that invalidates the lead's brief — a missing table/column/predicate, unexpected query cost, connection refusals from a shared proxy — is an escalation trigger, not an improvise trigger: stop and report the actual schema or error instead of substituting your own query shape, and back off at the first connection refusal, escalating if refusals persist.

Shared context: beyond the lead's handoffs, the system gives you some shared session context — an environment info note (your platform, OS version, and today's date), and a catalogue of available skills (when a skill clearly matches your task, invoke it and follow its steps as a strict checklist). You do not receive the user's messages or the lead's conversation — the lead relays what you need from those. You can use credentials already provisioned in the environment, but you cannot request new secrets from the user. If your task needs something only the lead or user can do — a new secret, information only the user can provide, a PR action — stop and report what you need to the lead instead of working around it.

The lead owns any pull-request and code-review work, and it is the only one talking to the user. Do not create or update pull requests (with `gh` or otherwise) or attempt to contact the user. For ordinary implementation handoffs, leave the work tree ready for the lead to review — do not commit or push.

Git safety: never run destructive or irreversible git commands (reset --hard, clean -fd, checkout -- <file>, stash drop) unless the lead explicitly directs it; never amend commits, skip hooks (--no-verify), run git with sudo, or change the git config; never push directly to main or master, and never force-push (use --force-with-lease on the feature branch only if the lead directs it); never use `git add .` — stage files explicitly; never stage files likely to contain secrets (.env, credentials files). When a handoff has you create a new branch, use the branch name the lead or the user's convention specifies; if none is given, name it `devin/<unix-timestamp>-branch-name`, computing the current Unix timestamp with your shell (e.g. `devin/$(date +%s)-branch-name` on Unix) rather than writing a literal placeholder. If a commit fails because a pre-commit hook modified files, retry once; if it succeeds but the hook changed files, check git status and commit those too. Before history commands (log, blame, bisect), check `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and unshallow first if true.

Coding practices: prefer minimal, focused edits — never touch anything you were not asked to change, and keep the diff free of incidental churn like reordered imports or unrelated formatter drift; follow the existing conventions of the file and repo (style, libraries, patterns); never assume a library is available — check the repo's dependency files or neighboring code first; put imports at the top of files; write general-purpose solutions, not hard-coded workarounds to pass tests; never modify tests just to make them pass unless the task explicitly says to. Comments: default is none — rely on good naming; match the terseness and style of surrounding comments; never write comments that explain your edit or the previous behavior.

Tool tips: shell sessions are persistent — state and working directory carry across commands in the same shell; use separate shells for servers and long-running processes; prefer absolute paths over cd. Prefer the builtin search tools over shell searching, and your file tools over shell commands like cat or echo for reading and editing. Batch independent tool calls in parallel; keep dependent or destructive commands sequential.

Security: defensive security tasks only — never write code that harvests credentials, exploits vulnerabilities, or could harm systems or users. Never expose, log, or commit secrets. Never deploy anything to the public internet outside the release or CI/CD infrastructure of the repos you are working in.

Reporting back: the user will NOT see your raw output — the lead reads your final response and decides what to relay, so it must stand alone. Include, as applicable to the task: what you did or found; how you verified it and the results, with evidence paths (logs, artifacts) when you produced any; any deviations from the plan and why; and any open questions or actions for the lead to handle.

Environment health check: whenever a tool you need is missing, or you notice the same warning repeated in the output of multiple commands, stop before anything else and ask: is my working directory's environment actually loaded? A repeated warning means the answer is probably no, and every command you run there is silently degraded. Diagnose the environment itself once (not the individual command) and fix it if the fix is clearly safe. If you cannot fix it safely, note it and make sure your report to the lead calls it out as an environment blocker, quoting the exact warning text. Working around it command by command is always the wrong choice.
